items.title: UN climate talks slammed by activists, leaders as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft agreement
items.summary: ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year’s U.N. climate summit reaches its final day. Friday marks the official end of this year’s two-week summit, known as COP31, which so far has failed to advance the drastic emission cuts needed to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change. Negotiators in Turkey expect the talks to go into overtime on Saturday. Civil society groups have warned this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever” if fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement. By Suzan Fraser, Anton L. items.title: Japan looks to offshore wind to boost energy security, but hurdles remain
items.summary: Japan has “tremendous potential” for offshore wind power, according to the national government and experts. But achieving that potential means overcoming major hurdles. While commercial-scale projects began coming online in recent years, the country still needs to address challenges that include refining its public-private partnerships, a buildout of related industries (such as turbine production), and involving local communities. However, tapping into offshore wind as a primary sustainable domestic energy source is critical to Japan, with the country’s energy self-sufficiency rate standing at just 16.4% in fiscal year 2024. The country’s first commercial offshore wind farms came online in Akita prefecture, at the ports of Noshiro and Akita, in 2022 and 2023 respectively. These wind farms, along with others that have come online since, currently generate 0.5 gigawatts of electricity, with capacity for a total of 5.7 GW by March 2031 if projects currently in the pipeline proceed as planned. But the nascent industry remains in its infancy. “Japan’s offshore wind power policy is currently at a very important turning point,” notes a team of experts from the Renewable Energy Institute (REI), a Japanese think tank. items.title: Floating wind is building ‘A lot of momentum’ toward commercialization
items.summary: It’s a little-known, nascent sustainable technology on the verge of commercialization: Floating wind turbines deployed across deep ocean waters could unlock vast amounts of renewable energy in the coming decades. For some countries (including China, Japan, South Korea, the U.K. and EU), floating wind is already playing a role in plans to decarbonize national economies, owing either to a lack of viable fixed-bottom offshore wind sites, or due to limited space for land-based renewables. For now, the emerging floating wind industry consists chiefly of small-scale demonstration and pilot projects, totaling around 300 megawatts (MW) of global output, a capacity dwarfed by current worldwide fixed wind generation at nearly 100 gigawatts (GW). The largest floating wind farm currently is Hywind Tampen in Norway with 11 floating turbines producing 94.6 MW for use by oil and gas installations. Despite its current lack of scale, Louise Efthimiou, the floating offshore wind manager at World Forum Offshore Wind, still sees floating wind “as a very strong contender” for decarbonization, albeit on a smaller scale than fixed offshore sites. “We can acknowledge that floating wind will not necessarily represent the bulk of offshore wind,” she told Mongabay in a video interview. “But it does benefit markets who don’t have the choice to do other than floating wind … offshore because of their water depths and their environment.” The major hurdle is getting floating wind up and running at a commercial scale. “The technology works, but it’s still in a phase of innovation, and so that…This…

items.title: Last Javan rhino habitat caught between mining plans and relocation debate
items.summary: JAKARTA — Indonesian lawmakers and environmental groups are urging the government to revoke a mining map covering part of the waters around Ujung Kulon National Park, home to the world’s last surviving Javan rhinos. The calls were in response to a proposal by Hashim Djojohadikusumo, a mining and energy tycoon and the brother of President Prabowo Subianto, to move some Javan rhinos (Rhinoceros sondaicus) from Ujung Kulon at the western tip of Java to Alas Purwo National Park at the other end of the island. Hashim made the statement during the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Türkiye on Nov. 12, in his role as the Indonesian government’s special envoy for climate and energy. He cited natural disasters as a major threat to the species, making the need for a translocation necessary. “If there is a tsunami due to an earthquake or a volcanic eruption, our Javan rhinos can go extinct,” he said. The national park is located around 70 kilometers (43 miles) from Anak Krakatau, a highly active volcano in the Sunda Strait that’s the remnant of the famous Krakatau. An eruption in December 2018 sheared off part of the slope of Anak Krakatua, leading to a landslide that triggered a tsunami. The waves radiated to Java and Sumatra, killing more than 420 people on both islands. None of the 68 rhinos at Ujung Kulon were affected, it was reported at the time. items.title: One in four land reptiles depends on rock habitats. Lack of protection leaves them in a hard place
items.summary: More than a quarter of the world’s land reptiles depend on rocky habitats, yet these areas are often overlooked in conservation efforts, according to a recent study. For cold-blooded lizards, snakes, and worm lizards (legless lizards), rocks often provide warmth for basking, shelter from predators, and places to hunt, socialize, and breed. However, the number of reptile species globally that use rocky habitats like cliffs, outcrops, or karst systems, and how threatened they are, still remains uncertain, researchers write in the study. To fill the gap, the researchers analyzed 9,729 terrestrial species belonging to the order Squamata, which includes all lizards, snakes, and worm lizards. For each species, they consulted the IUCN Red List, which documents its conservation status, habitat requirements, and threats. Their analysis found that 2,479 species, or more than 25% of those studied, use rocky habitats. Of these, 1,022 species, or 10.5%, were entirely dependent on rocks — that is, they lived almost exclusively on rocks and used rocks for breeding, shelter, and to regulate their temperature. Of the studied species that use rocks, nearly 30%, or 676 species, are classified as threatened on the IUCN Red List, the study found. Species that depend entirely on rocky habitats were 51% more likely to be critically endangered than those that use them only occasionally. items.title: Fossil fuels’ role in Africa’s energy transition contested as UN climate conference closes
items.summary: As the 2026 edition of the annual U.N. Climate Change Conference reaches its conclusion in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 20, African governments are arguing for increased financial and technical support to respond to climate change. Top priorities include more money for protection of forests and other landscapes, funding to help vulnerable communities and economies adapt to a changed climate, and financial backing for a just energy transition for fossil-fuel producing and consuming economies on the continent. Access to energy and what role remains for fossil fuels are contested topics, with many African governments planning continued reliance on coal, diesel and natural gas for transport, industry and electricity generation. Jane Mbabazi Byaruhanga, responsible for environmental and social affairs at Uganda’s Petroleum Authority, is among the thousands attending the summit. Africa’s households, schools, health centers and businesses lack access to affordable, reliable energy, she told Mongabay in a phone interview from Antalya. Two in five Ugandans lacked access to electricity from the national grid in 2025, according to government records; in rural areas, access was 43% of the population. This situation is mirrored across the continent: The International Energy Agency estimates that nearly 600 million of the continent’s 1.5 billion inhabitants do not have access to electricity. “Africa, to begin with, needs reliable and affordable energy to enhance their development, and we should always aim at the continent to have energy that is produced and also used responsibly,” she…

items.title: Nickel linked to deforestation in Indonesia traded on London Metal Exchange, says report
items.summary: Two companies approved for trading nickel on the London Metal Exchange (LME) could be linked to supply chains that have cleared primary rainforest in Indonesia, according to a report published by the NGO Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA). The NGO investigated two LME-approved Indonesian refiners – PT CNGR Ding Xing and PT Eternal Nickel Industry (ENI) – and traced each of their corporate ownerships to mines driving extensive deforestation across Sulawesi and the North Maluku islands. The investigation claims  that the companies’ supply chains were possibly linked to clearing up to 7,270 hectares (17,965 acres) of primary rainforest in Indonesia. Current LME rules require metal brands to comply with the OECD’s Due Diligence Guidelines, which provide government-backed management recommendations for “responsible supply chains of all minerals”, including their refined metal derivatives. However, the guidelines lack binding environmental criteria for deforestation, biodiversity loss or Indigenous land rights, according to the EIA.  “The LME has put in place solid requirements on metal sellers to address supply chain issues like conflict financing and child labour,” said Colin Robertson, EIA Forests Campaign lead for mining, told Mongabay over email. “Deforestation caused by mining is a growing problem and it seems to be a blind spot for the LME and for the mining and metals sector in general.” Neither company  publicly discloses its mine suppliers under current LMEpassport rules, the digital platform for recording and sharing information about the physical metal that…

items.title: As Nepal celebrates the crow, urban sprawl and waste drive strain
items.summary: Every year around the Hindu festival of Diwali, or Deepavali, residents in Nepal observe Kaag Tihar, an annual festival day dedicated to worshipping house crows as divine messengers. However, in the country’s capital, rapid urban sprawl, habitat degradation and changing perceptions toward the bird are testing human-crow relations, reports Mongabay’s Gobinda Pokharel. Satellite analysis shows Kathmandu’s urban build-up area expanded by 124% between 1989 and 2018, while another study found municipal green space plummeted by 54% between 1975 and 2025. Meanwhile, the removal of more than 2,000 mature trees along major thoroughfares like the Kathmandu Ring Road has forced house crows (Corvus splendens) to nest on utility poles and electrical wires, according to a 2024 study led by Tribhuvan University researcher Dinesh Bhusal, in Nepal. “When old and large trees are cut down, specialist birds lose their habitats,” said Hem Bahadur Katuwal, a bird ecologist at the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences, southwest China. “Eventually, only functional generalist species, such as crows, which can survive under almost any conditions, remain.” Compounding the population shift is Kathmandu’s unmanaged refuse. Open dumping of waste along riverbanks and uncovered trash at meat shops provide abundant forage, attracting dense concentrations of crows and black kites (Milvus migrans). “Large quantities of discarded food and exposed waste from meat shops have contributed to the unusual increase in crows and kites in Kathmandu,” said Kamal Raj Gosai, an…

items.title: The long reach of El Niño impacts on Southeast Asia’s primates
items.summary: As Indonesia’s El-Niño driven fires spark a race to save endangered orangutans and other wildlife, a recent review paper, published in the journal Oryx, is raising concerns about both the short- and long-term impacts on primates of such climatic events in Southeast Asia. “Primates might survive a fire, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us whether they’re going to have enough food or suitable habitat, or what’s happening with their health and ability to reproduce in the months and years ahead,” said Elizabeth Barrow, lead author of the paper and conservation research director at the Gunung Palung Orangutan Conservation Program (GPOCP), Indonesia. With 94% of Southeast Asia’s primates threatened with extinction, the impact of El Niño is a poorly understood but significant threat to populations, according to the researchers. “From my perspective, this is a huge conservation issue for primates in Southeast Asia,” Barrow said. Habitat loss and degradation caused by drought and fire are linked to several concerning impacts. They can drive changes in diet, behavior and the physical condition of primates, the review found. Primate populations can become crowded as forest areas shrink, while others may be displaced, suffer localized extirpations, or increased infant mortality. In total, however, the review identified only 15 papers on the impacts of El Niño-linked drought, fire and smoke on primates. items.title: Catching more plastic than fish in Sierra Leone’s coastal Mahera
items.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — On a rainy Saturday morning, 57-year-old fisher Sheriff Kamara sat among other community members inside a wooden makeshift shelter in Sierra Leone’s Mahera Beach, waiting for the weather to improve. Along the shoreline, discarded plastic bottles, water sachets, bags and food wrappers lay scattered among old footwear and foam. For Kamara, plastic waste has become a regular problem, increasingly affecting his ability to fish and earn a living. “When I started fishing, it was rare to find anything in my net besides fish. But now, it is a weekly, sometimes a daily, problem,” he tells Mongabay. According to Kamara, a lot of single-use plastic waste frequently gets caught in his fishing nets, particularly near the shore after a heavy rain. Removing the entangled plastic waste takes considerable time and effort. “I find all sorts of plastic in my net almost every week. Removing the plastics with my apprentice’s help takes a lot of time,” he says. For fishermen like him, plastic pollution is not just an environmental concern but an additional burden on their daily work and livelihoods. To support the fishing communities, the government launched a fisheries and marine resources strategy in 2025, which provides a 10-year framework for promoting sustainable fisheries management, protecting marine ecosystems and improving livelihoods. It also calls for sustainable use of marine resources and stronger protection for the fisheries sector. items.t: Catching more plastic than fish in Sierra Leone’s coastal Mahera

items.title: Peruvian officials reportedly increase tally to more than 12,000 tarantulas in recent seizure
items.summary: Peruvian authorities have updated the number of tarantulas seized in a recent wildlife trafficking case from 3,000 to more than 12,000, according to South American media reports. The final count of 12,796 seized spiders was reportedly announced by the Peruvian National Police (PNP). The authorities said they believe these arachnids are worth more than half a million euros (around $548,000) on the international market. On Nov. 4, 2026, the Peruvian National Forest and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) announced it seized thousands of tarantulas at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima, hidden inside socks and plastic containers in luggage destined for Germany. Authorities arrested two German citizens and a Polish national, including a “renowned tarantula researcher” who was not publicly identified, and detained them for further investigation at the time. The seized tarantulas included individuals in different life stages, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, and came from across Peru. They included blue bird eaters (Thrixopelma lagunas), Bolivian blue leg bird eater (Pamphobeteus antinous), members of the genus Pamphobeteus  and several newly described species. Authorities said the alleged traffickers collected the spiders from the wild to sell as exotic pets to collectors and for research. None of the seized species are internationally protected under CITES, the global wildlife treaty. items.title: Geopolitical tensions hamper efforts to curb overfishing in waters near Europe
items.summary: LONDON — On Nov. 10, Mongabay went to the site of the annual meeting of the body that regulates fishing in the northeastern Atlantic, where a little-known geopolitical dispute over marine resources was playing out behind closed doors. The North-East Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC), a multilateral body, governs the fishing of three major stocks of fish in international waters near Europe, as well as associated species and habitats. Disagreement between countries over how to manage the stocks has had serious consequences, experts say. All three species — Atlantic mackerel (Scomber scombrus), Atlanto-Scandian herring (Clupea harengus), and blue whiting (Micromesistius poutassou) — have been subject to overfishing for years. The Northeast Atlantic mackerel population is in particularly bad shape, currently 22% below the NEAFC’s target threshold, having been fished above scientifically advised levels every year since 2008. The NEAFC is one of the world’s 17 regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs), and a fisheries governance campaigner has called it the most “fraught” and “problematic.” It has six member parties: the European Union, the United Kingdom, Iceland, Norway, Russia, and Denmark (on behalf of the Faroe Islands and Greenland; the delegation is commonly called DFG). The three fish species are prey for marine mammals and seabirds, and are sought after on global markets. items.title: 44 Astonishing Photos Of The Animal Kingdom’s Hunters, Shared By Wildlife Photographers
items.summary:
In the wild, a single photograph can tell a story of patience, instinct, and survival. A tiny spider carrying its catch, an eagle gripping its meal high above the ground, or a big cat standing proudly beside its latest hunt - these are fleeting scenes that reveal a side of the animal kingdom we don't often get to witness up close. And while nature is full of beautiful sights, some of its most compelling moments are far less predictable.

items.title: Central-north Amazonia has experienced an ‘alarming’ increase in temperatures: Study
items.summary: A small team of scientists was counting plants for a forest census near Manaus in northern Brazil when fire season started in October 2023. Some days the smoke was too thick to see; on other days it was too hot to wear conventional masks, so Aretha Guimarães, a biologist with Brazil’s National Institute of Amazonian Research (INPA) and her colleagues covered their faces with wet bandages in order to breathe. Even through the bandages and smoke, the smell of dead, rotting sloths was overpowering, Guimarães remembers. “Animals just kept showing up dead,” she told Mongabay over a video call. “I’ve never seen such mortality. We were shocked.” Over the following months, Guimarães and her team found dead sloths in every part of the forest they studied; some still hanging from branches. Most, they assumed, could not move quickly enough to find water when temperatures started to rise. “I can’t explain what happened, because I’ve never seen such a thing.” For decades, research has highlighted southern Amazonia, thousands of kilometers away, as the region’s climate change hotspot, where average temperatures are increasing faster than the north, exacerbated by deforestation and sweeping forest fires. items.title: Threatened species make up half of shark catches at Indonesian fishing port, study finds

However, their value to fishing communities comes at a cost to conservation: Threatened species, including the critically endangered scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), made up a substantial share of the sharks landed at Muncar. A study published earlier this year in the journal Oryx examined shark catches landed in Muncar between 2023 and 2024. Researchers combined catch records with interviews with fishers, landing data, and GPS data to investigate which species were caught, where fishing took place, and which practices posed the greatest risks to threatened species. The findings revealed a worrying pattern. According to the study, 50% of recorded shark catches comprised species classified as threatened on the Red List of the IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority. A third of species were listed on CITES, which regulates the global trade in protected wildlife. Scalloped hammerheads accounted for 11.7% of recorded catches. items.title: Skinks in boots: How Hong Kong emerges as key hub in Australia’s native reptile trafficking
items.summary: HONG KONG — Two days after Christmas last year, customs authorities at Hong Kong International Airport intercepted a consignment from Australia and found 13 live lizards bound and stuffed inside sheepskin winter shoes, popularly known as ugg boots. The air cargo was falsely declared to contain snacks, Hong Kong’s Customs said in a press release in late December 2025. But instead, inside were assorted lizard species, including the shingleback skink (Tiliqua rugosa). Between March 2025 and July 2026, Customs announced at least three other seizures of live reptiles found in consignments from Australia. In the four cases, customs officers confiscated 98 live animals — 74 lizards and 24 snakes — with the total value exceeding 1.1 million Hong Kong dollars ($141,100). All but one lizard were believed to be listed in the global wildlife trade convention CITES appendices. According to Hong Kong authorities, most of these seizures are under investigation, and one was dropped. No arrests have been made. Despite Australia’s comprehensive ban on commercial exports of live native species since 1982, the rarity and unique looks of its reptiles have made them coveted in pet markets around the world. items.title: World Anteater Day: Rewilding and restoration offer hope for enigmatic species
items.summary: World Anteater Day falls on Nov. 19, in recognition of the tube-nosed, ant- and termite-eating animals living across Central and South America. Closely related to sloths, anteaters generally live in trees. The largest species, the giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla), lives on the ground, though, where it rips open anthills and termite nests with its razor-sharp claws and slurps up the insects with its long, sticky tongue. A giant anteater’s return in Argentina offers a case for letting nature restore itself In 2025, a giant anteater returned to the Alma Guaraní reserve in Argentina’s Gran Chaco region for the first known time since 1986, reported Mongabay contributor Sean Mowbray. items.title: Britain’s birds stay closer to home amid mild winters
items.summary:
Smaller species such as swallows and skylarks are more likely to stay near breeding grounds rather than migrate

Bonfire Night is over, Christmas is coming, and Britain’s birds are getting ready for the winter. They must survive the extremes of our weather and make it through to next spring to get the chance to breed again.

Birds have very different strategies to prepare for cold weather. Many smaller birds – swallows and swifts, cuckoos and chats, warblers and flycatchers – simply avoid it by migrating: some fly all the way to sub-Saharan Africa, where they enjoy the benefits of a second spring and summer south of the equator. Others, such as blackbirds and robins, stay put. But if they sense that a cold spell is coming, they too will head south, though not as far – most either remain in south-west Britain or cross the Channel to France or Spain.

A bar-tailed godwit called Phil has completed a 6,800-mile journey from Norfolk to Siberia and back again, in the first UK mapping of the endurance feats of this long-distance migrant.

A wading bird not much larger than a pigeon, the bar-tailed godwit is known for making the longest recorded non-stop migratory flight of any bird. Populations that visit Britain spend summers breeding in the Arctic Circle before retreating to the unfrozen wetlands of Britain in winter. (AP) — Officials at Grand Canyon National Park announced Wednesday that they are easing water restrictions, meaning hotels on the South Rim will once again be able to accommodate overnight guests. The famous El Tovar Hotel along with several other lodges will reopen Friday now that the park has reached a milestone in restoration of water service following severe flooding earlier this year. Flooding in late August caused three deaths, prompted rescues and damaged key infrastructure, including a water intake pump and a significant stretch of a decades-old pipeline that supplied water for millions of visitors to the South Rim and about 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village. At the time, officials said they were just over a month away from completing a more than $200 million upgrade to the 12.5-mile-long (20-kilometer) Transcanyon Waterline. More flooding in September damaged temporary repairs. Although lodging is reopening, park officials urge visitors to conserve as restoration of the water system continues. “Simple actions, including taking shorter showers, turning off faucets when not in use and avoiding unnecessary water use, help support the park’s water system as operations resume,” the park said in its announcement. Food and beverage services will resume gradually, according to park officials. By Associated Press Banner image: The Grand Canyon. On the morning of Aug. 26, 2026, a catastrophic flood began with a rock and ice collapse on the northern flank of Langtang Lirung, within Langtang National Park. The park is one of country’s major Himalayan protected areas and provides habitat for species like Himalayan musk deer (Moschus leucogaster), Asiatic black bear (Ursus thibetanus), red panda (Ailurus fulgens) and clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa). Then, on Oct. 11, another destructive flood occurred in the Budhi Gandaki basin after a landslide blocked the river near Chumchet village in Gorkha District within the Manaslu Conservation Area that supports snow leopard (Panthera uncia), musk deer, blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur) and Himalayan tahr (Hemitragus jemlahicus), along with more than 200 recorded Himalayan plant species. In the Himalaya, because of the extraordinary diversity and interconnectedness, any disturbance created in a high mountain valley can affect forests, wetlands and floodplains much further downstream. Hunters used scent hounds to track game through forests, truffle hunters in Italy bred dogs to find fungi buried underground, and today dogs help find explosives, drugs, and even signs of some diseases. Now, scientists in Germany have given them a new kind of target: invasive plants.

Dogs are being trained to detect invasive plants before they spread and threaten local ecosystems

Researchers from the Helmholtz Center for Environmental Research (UFZ) in Leipzig set out to test whether ordinary pet dogs and their owners could be trained to find invasive plant species in the wild. The results were encouraging. In a final field test, the volunteer teams located their target plants with an average success rate of 75%. The findings were published in the scientific journal PLOS ONE in November 2026. 

Invasive species may not get as much attention as climate change, but their impact is enormous. According to a 2023 global assessment by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), invasive species have been a major factor in 60% of recorded plant and animal extinctions, and they cost the world more than $423 billion in 2019 alone. Once an invasive plant takes hold, it can spread rapidly, crowd out native species, and change the habitats wildlife depends on.

items.title: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters
items.summary:
Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations

Your article (Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century.

There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that does not necessarily make predator-free conditions either natural or desirable. Restoring eagles is not simply about recovering a charismatic species; it is about restoring lost ecological relationships and processes.
